title: Molecular Signals That Pattern the Embryo
summary: The signaling pathways and gene networks that tell cells where they are and what to become.

lessons.title: Morphogen Gradients: Shh, Wnt, BMP, FGF and Retinoic Acid

levels.kid:
Imagine a campfire in a dark field. Kids sitting close feel very warm. Kids far away feel only a little warmth. Just by feeling the heat, each kid knows how far they are from the fire.

A growing baby uses the same trick! Some cells give off special signal chemicals called **morphogens**. Cells near the source get a lot of the signal. Cells far away get only a little.

Each cell "reads" how much it gets and decides what to become. A lot might mean "become this kind of nerve cell." A little might mean "become a different kind."

A few of these signals have funny names, like **Sonic hedgehog**, named after a video game hero! Together, these signals help build a body with everything in the right place.
levels.hs:
A **morphogen** is a signaling molecule that spreads out from a source and forms a **concentration gradient**: high near the source, lower farther away. Cells respond differently depending on how much they receive. This lets one signal create several cell types in an orderly pattern. Biologists call this "positional information."

A classic idea is the **French flag model** (Lewis Wolpert, 1969). Picture a row of cells. Above one threshold, cells turn "blue." Between two thresholds, they turn "white." Below both, they turn "red." Three stripes come from one gradient.

Five signal families do much of this work in human embryos:
- **Sonic hedgehog (Shh)**: patterns the spinal cord and the digits of the hand.
- **Wnt**: helps set up the head-to-tail axis and posterior structures.
- **BMP (bone morphogenetic protein)**: patterns the back-to-belly (dorsal-ventral) axis.
- **FGF (fibroblast growth factor)**: drives growth, including limb outgrowth.
- **Retinoic acid (RA)**: a vitamin A derivative that helps pattern the trunk.

Real example: in the developing spinal cord, the **notochord** and **floor plate** release Shh at the ventral (belly) side. Cells closest to it become floor plate and **motor neurons**. Cells farther away become interneurons. Meanwhile, BMP from the dorsal (back) side makes sensory-related neurons. The two opposing gradients divide the neural tube into distinct zones.
levels.college:
Morphogens act directly, at a distance, and in a dose-dependent way, specifying at least two cell fates by thresholds. Gradients form through local production, spread by diffusion or transport, and removal through degradation or receptor uptake.

**The five major families and their logic:**
- **Shh**: secreted from the notochord, floor plate and the limb's **zone of polarizing activity (ZPA)**. It binds **Patched (PTCH1)**, which relieves Patched's inhibition of **Smoothened (SMO)**. This shifts **Gli** transcription factors from repressor to activator forms. Shh is cholesterol-modified, which affects how it spreads.
- **Wnt**: in the canonical pathway, Wnt binds Frizzled/LRP5/6. This blocks the destruction complex (APC, Axin, GSK3β), so **β-catenin** builds up and enters the nucleus with TCF/LEF. High posterior Wnt promotes trunk and tail fates; anterior Wnt antagonists such as Dkk1 protect the head.
- **BMP**: TGF-β superfamily ligands signal through serine/threonine kinase receptors that phosphorylate **SMAD1/5/8**. In gastrulation, organizer-derived antagonists (**Noggin, Chordin, Follistatin**) block BMP dorsally, allowing neural tissue to form. That is why ectoderm with low BMP becomes neural.
- **FGF**: receptor tyrosine kinases (FGFR1-4) activate the **Ras-MAPK** pathway. FGF8/FGF10 loops between the **apical ectodermal ridge (AER)** and limb mesenchyme drive limb outgrowth.
- **Retinoic acid**: made from retinol by **RALDH2** (ALDH1A2) and broken down by **CYP26** enzymes. RA enters the nucleus and binds **RAR/RXR** receptors, which act directly as transcription factors.

**Opposing gradients**: posterior FGF/Wnt and anterior RA antagonize each other along the body axis. In the neural tube, ventral Shh opposes dorsal BMP/Wnt.

**Clinical link**: loss of Shh signaling causes **holoprosencephaly**. Too much RA is strongly teratogenic, as with isotretinoin. Ectopic Shh in the anterior limb produces mirror-image extra digits.
levels.phd:
The ventral neural tube is the best-quantified vertebrate morphogen system. Shh from the notochord and floor plate specifies five ventral progenitor domains (p0, p1, p2, pMN, p3) through **class I** genes (Pax6, Irx3, Dbx), which Shh represses, and **class II** genes (Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1, Olig2), which Shh induces. Briscoe, Ericson, Jessell and colleagues showed that boundaries are sharpened by **cross-repressive pairs** (Pax6/Nkx2.2, Olig2/Irx3). The gradient therefore acts as an initial bias, and a bistable transcriptional network converts it into crisp, heritable states.

**Time matters as much as concentration.** Dessaud et al. (2007) proposed **temporal adaptation**: cells desensitize over time partly through Shh-induced Ptch1 upregulation, so exposure duration, not just peak level, sets fate. Ventral fates need both higher and longer signaling. Gli activity, not ligand level, is the relevant read-out.

**Gradient formation remains debated.** Options include free diffusion with degradation (Fgf8 in zebrafish; Yu et al. 2009 used fluorescence correlation spectroscopy), restricted extracellular diffusion shaped by heparan sulfate proteoglycans, transcytosis, and **cytonemes**, filopodia that deliver ligand directly (Kornberg; Shh in chick limb). Shh's dual lipidation (C-terminal cholesterol, N-terminal palmitate via Hhat) requires Dispatched and Scube2 for release. A simple synthesis-diffusion-degradation model gives an exponential profile, C(x) = C₀e^(−x/λ) with λ = √(D/k). This structure explains why positional precision falls with distance from the source.

**Source-sink systems**: RA shows that gradients can be shaped by enzymes rather than ligand movement. Localized RALDH2 production and CYP26 degradation in anterior and tail tissues make a self-sharpening profile. FGF8 mRNA decays as cells leave the tailbud, so the gradient is "inherited" through mRNA decay rather than diffusion (Dubrulle and Pourquié 2004).

**Limb ZPA nuance**: Harfe et al. (2004) showed that posterior digits derive from Shh-expressing cells themselves. Digit identity therefore depends on both concentration and duration of exposure, combining a morphogen model and a timing model rather than Wolpert's pure concentration reading.

**Scaling** of gradients to tissue size (e.g., via expander-repressor feedback) remains an open problem.
levels.expert:
Clinically, morphogen biology is mostly encountered through its failures, and the phenotypes map onto pathways with useful precision.

**Holoprosencephaly (HPE)**, the most common human forebrain malformation, follows from reduced midline Shh. Contributors include heterozygous **SHH**, ZIC2, SIX3 and TGIF1 variants and defects in cholesterol synthesis. In **Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome** (DHCR7 deficiency), defective sterol handling impairs Smoothened activation as well as ligand processing. Penetrance is strikingly variable even within families. A multiple-hit model, combining a dosage-sensitive variant, modifier genes and environmental Shh antagonism, fits better than single-gene causation. The plant alkaloid **cyclopamine**, which causes cyclopic lambs in sheep grazing *Veratrum*, binds Smoothened directly. This veterinary toxicology finding opened the field of Hh pharmacology.

**Pharmacology tie-in.** Vismodegib, sonidegib and glasdegib are SMO antagonists used in basal cell carcinoma and AML. Their strict pregnancy prevention requirements follow directly from developmental biology. Resistance arises through SMO mutations or downstream GLI amplification, the same logic as Gli acting as the true read-out. **SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma**, a key neurosurgical tumor, recapitulates cerebellar granule-precursor proliferation driven by Purkinje-cell Shh. PTCH1 mutations respond to SMO inhibition; SUFU and GLI2 lesions do not. SMO inhibitors can also cause permanent growth-plate fusion in children, a developmental side effect seen in trials.

**Retinoid embryopathy** (isotretinoin) affects craniofacial, conotruncal cardiac, thymic and CNS structures. These are the neural-crest and hindbrain territories most sensitive to RA levels. Both RA excess and RA deficiency are harmful, consistent with the source-sink logic of RA patterning.

**Research frontiers:**
- **Stem-cell organoids and gastruloids** now let investigators impose morphogen gradients with microfluidics or optogenetics, testing which cell fates follow from gradient shape.
- **Ventral spinal cord differentiation protocols** (RA plus Shh agonist such as SAG/purmorphamine for motor neurons) are direct applications of the gradient code. They now underpin ALS disease modeling and cell-replacement work.
- **Live single-cell imaging** quantifies how precise positional information really is. Measurements suggest that combining opposing gradients improves positional accuracy beyond what either gradient achieves alone.

**Open questions**: how gradients scale with growth, how noise is buffered, and how ligand transport mechanisms (diffusion vs. cytonemes) differ across tissues *in vivo*.

keyPoints: A morphogen forms a concentration gradient that specifies different fates at different thresholds
Wolpert's French flag model: one gradient, several cell types
Shh patterns ventral neural tube and limb digits via Patched, Smoothened and Gli
BMP patterns the dorsal-ventral axis; organizer antagonists (Noggin, Chordin) allow neural fate
Wnt/β-catenin, FGF (Ras-MAPK) and retinoic acid (RAR/RXR) pattern the head-tail axis and limbs
Duration of exposure and cross-repressive gene networks sharpen gradient read-outs

test.q: What best defines a morphogen?
choices: An enzyme that breaks down a used growth factor
A gene copied identically into each embryonic cell
A signal giving different fates at different concentrations
A structural protein holding embryonic cells together
test.explain: Morphogens form gradients, and cells adopt different fates depending on the concentration they receive.

test.q: In the neural tube, which structures secrete Sonic hedgehog ventrally?
test.explain: The notochord and floor plate are the ventral Shh sources. The roof plate is a dorsal BMP/Wnt source.

test.q: Cells closest to the ventral Shh source in the spinal cord tend to become:
test.explain: High Shh specifies the most ventral fates, such as floor plate and motor neurons.

test.q: Organizer proteins Noggin and Chordin allow ectoderm to become neural by:
test.explain: These antagonists bind BMP and block it. Ectoderm with low BMP becomes neural tissue.

test.q: In canonical Wnt signaling, which protein builds up and enters the nucleus?
test.explain: Wnt inhibits the destruction complex, so β-catenin accumulates and partners with TCF/LEF in the nucleus.

test.q: What kind of receptor do FGFs bind?
test.explain: FGFR1-4 are receptor tyrosine kinases that activate Ras-MAPK. Serine/threonine kinase receptors are used by BMP.

test.q: Retinoic acid acts inside cells by binding:
test.explain: RA is a small lipophilic molecule that binds nuclear receptors RAR/RXR, which act directly as transcription factors.

test.q: Placing extra Shh in the anterior limb bud typically causes:
test.explain: Ectopic Shh mimics a second ZPA and creates mirror-image digit duplications.

test.q: Reduced Shh signaling in the midline is linked to which malformation?
test.explain: Holoprosencephaly, failure of the forebrain to divide, results from reduced midline Shh. Polydactyly, such as preaxial polydactyly, is more typical of excess Shh.

test.q: Wolpert's ___ flag model explains how one gradient makes three cell types.
test.explain: The French flag model uses two thresholds to create blue, white and red zones.

test.q: What limb signaling center at the posterior edge produces Shh? (abbreviation)
test.explain: The zone of polarizing activity is the Shh source that patterns the digits.

test.q: Retinoic acid is made from vitamin ___.
test.explain: RA is a derivative of vitamin A (retinol), produced by the enzyme RALDH2.

kidTest.q: What is a morphogen?
choices: A tiny bone inside a baby's hand
A food the baby eats to grow
A signal chemical that cells can sense
kidTest.explain: Morphogens are signal chemicals that spread out from a source.

kidTest.q: Cells close to the signal source get:
kidTest.explain: Like warmth near a campfire, the signal is strongest close to the source.

kidTest.q: How does a cell decide what to become?
choices: By reading how much signal it gets
By copying the cell above it
By counting the cells around it
kidTest.explain: The amount of signal tells the cell what job to take.

kidTest.q: Sonic hedgehog was named after a:
kidTest.explain: Scientists named this signal after the video game character Sonic.

kidTest.q: In the story, kids feel warmth from a camp _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The campfire is like the signal source: warmer close by, cooler far away.

advancedTest.q: Ptch1 upregulation by Shh contributes to temporal adaptation because it:
choices: Sequesters ligand and desensitizes cells over time
Turns Gli repressors into stable nuclear activators
Speeds diffusion of Shh away from the floor plate
Raises SMO activity so that cells keep responding
advancedTest.explain: Patched is both a receptor and an inhibitor; its induction dampens signaling. Fate then reflects both duration and level of exposure.

advancedTest.q: In C(x)=C₀e^(−x/λ) with λ=√(D/k), raising the degradation rate k would:
choices: Leave the gradient shape unchanged overall
Steepen the gradient and shorten its range
Broaden the gradient and extend its range
Raise the concentration at the source alone
advancedTest.explain: A larger k reduces λ, so the concentration falls off more quickly with distance from the source.

advancedTest.q: An SHH medulloblastoma with a SUFU loss would likely resist SMO inhibitors because:
choices: SUFU loss switches cells to Wnt signaling
The lesion lies downstream of Smoothened
SUFU loss raises Patched receptor levels
SUFU loss blocks drug entry into the brain
advancedTest.explain: SUFU acts downstream of SMO, so the pathway stays active even when SMO is blocked. PTCH1-mutant tumors, by contrast, respond to SMO inhibition.

advancedTest.q: Cross-repression between Pax6 and Nkx2.2 matters in neural tube patterning because it:
choices: Speeds the spread of Shh to dorsal cells
Turns a graded input into sharp, stable domains
Makes the gradient form without degradation
Lets one cell sense two morphogens equally
advancedTest.explain: Mutual repression creates bistable switches that convert a noisy gradient into crisp, heritable boundaries.

lessons.title: Hox Genes and Anterior-Posterior Identity

levels.kid:
Your body is built like a long train. The front car is your head, then come your neck, chest, belly and hips. Each car looks a bit different. How does each part know which car it is?

Inside every cell is a set of special instructions called **Hox genes**. Think of them as address labels. Cells near your head switch on the first labels. Cells farther back switch on more labels. The label that comes last in the line is the one that matters most for that spot.

Here is a cool surprise. The Hox genes sit in a row on the DNA, in the same order as the body parts they label, from head to tail! Flies, mice and people all use these same address labels.
levels.hs:
Every animal with a front and a back must solve a problem: how does a cell know whether it should help build a neck, a ribcage or a lower back? Part of the answer is a family of genes called **Hox genes**.

Hox genes make **transcription factors**, proteins that switch other genes on or off. Each Hox protein contains a 60-amino-acid region called the **homeodomain** that grips DNA. Together, the Hox genes active in a cell act like a postal code for its position along the **anterior-posterior (A-P) axis**, the head-to-tail line.

Key features:
- Humans have **39 Hox genes** in four clusters, called HOXA, HOXB, HOXC and HOXD, on four different chromosomes.
- Genes are arranged on the chromosome in the same order as the body regions they pattern. This is called **colinearity**.
- In posterior regions, the more posterior genes usually take charge. This is called **posterior prevalence**.

The discovery came from fruit flies. In the **Antennapedia** mutant, legs grow where antennae should be. In **bithorax** mutants, a fly grows a second pair of wings. Changing a body part into another part's identity is called a **homeotic transformation**.

Vertebrae show Hox control clearly. Neck vertebrae have no ribs, chest vertebrae do, and Hox codes help decide which is which.
levels.college:
Hox genes are the best-studied system for assigning **regional identity** along the A-P axis. They do not build structures directly. Instead they tell already-formed tissues such as somites, hindbrain segments and neural crest what kind of structure to become.

**Organization.** Mammals have 39 Hox genes in four clusters (HOXA on chromosome 7, HOXB on 17, HOXC on 12, HOXD on 2 in humans). These clusters arose from duplications of an ancestral cluster. Genes are sorted into **13 paralog groups**. For example, Hoxa4, Hoxb4, Hoxc4 and Hoxd4 form paralog group 4, and members of a group often share functions.

**Colinearity.** It works in three ways:
- **Spatial**: 3' genes (groups 1-2) are expressed more anteriorly, while 5' genes (groups 10-13) are expressed more posteriorly.
- **Temporal**: 3' genes switch on earlier during gastrulation. 5' genes switch on later as the axis elongates.
- **Quantitative**: more 5' genes tend to be expressed at higher levels in a nested pattern.

**Upstream control.** Retinoic acid activates 3' Hox genes, which helps set hindbrain and cervical identities. Posterior Wnt and FGF signaling, together with **Cdx** transcription factors, push on more 5' genes.

**Readout examples.**
- **Hindbrain**: Hoxa1/Hoxb1 and later groups 2-4 give rhombomeres distinct identities. These identities shape cranial nerve nuclei and the pharyngeal arches seeded by neural crest.
- **Axial skeleton**: Hox6 genes are associated with the cervical-thoracic transition. Hox10 genes block rib formation to make lumbar vertebrae, and Hox11 genes specify sacral identity.
- **Limbs**: Hoxd9-13 and Hoxa9-13 pattern the stylopod, zeugopod and autopod (Hox10, Hox11 and Hox13 respectively).

**Partners.** Hox proteins bind DNA weakly and with low specificity on their own. **TALE cofactors**, Pbx and Meis, raise their specificity. Loss of Hox function often produces **anterior homeotic transformations**, in which a segment adopts the identity of the segment in front of it.
levels.phd:
**Homeodomain biochemistry.** The 60-residue homeodomain is a helix-turn-helix. Helix 3 reads the major groove, and the N-terminal arm contacts the minor groove. Most Hox homeodomains recognize similar TAAT-containing cores, which creates the "Hox specificity paradox." Studies from Mann, Honig and colleagues showed that Pbx-Hox heterodimers unmask **latent specificity**. Anterior Hox proteins favor binding sites with a narrower minor groove, read by basic residues (DNA shape readout). They also tolerate **low-affinity sites**, which are essential for specific enhancer output in vivo; converting these to high-affinity sites causes ectopic activation.

**Genetic logic.** Paralog redundancy hid much of this system at first. Single knockouts give subtle phenotypes. The Capecchi lab's paralog-group knockouts were striking: in Wellik and Capecchi (2003), loss of all Hox10 genes produced ribs on every lumbar vertebra. Loss of all Hox11 genes turned sacral vertebrae into lumbar-like ones. In limbs, Hox11 loss strongly disrupted the radius and ulna, and Hoxa13/Hoxd13 loss eliminated the autopod. **Posterior prevalence** (Duboule's term) explains why posterior genes dominate phenotypically, partly through functional suppression of anterior inputs.

**Chromatin and temporal colinearity.** Before activation, the clusters are covered by Polycomb-associated H3K27me3. Duboule's lab showed that during axial extension the clusters transition progressively, 3' to 5', into an active compartment marked by H3K4me3. This occurs alongside 3D chromatin reorganization. The transition links the order of genes on the chromosome to their activation time. CTCF sites within HoxA and HoxD act as boundaries that pace this progression. Deleting them shifts expression boundaries and vertebral identities.

**Regulatory landscapes.** The HoxD cluster lies between two TADs (topologically associating domains). The telomeric TAD drives early proximal limb expression, and the centromeric TAD drives late digit expression. This **bimodal switch** produces a Hoxd-low wrist zone, a mechanism likely co-opted when vertebrates evolved hands and feet.

**Microcolinearity in the head.** Hoxa2 is the only Hox gene expressed in second-arch neural crest. The first arch is Hox-negative, and this Hox-free ground state is required for the jaw. Loss of Hoxa2 transforms second-arch skeletal elements into a mirror duplicate of first-arch elements.
levels.expert:
**Human Hox disorders are rare and usually partial.** Redundancy shields most HOX loss-of-function. Recognized syndromes involve highly sensitive dosage points:
- **HOXD13**: synpolydactyly type II, caused by polyalanine tract expansions with dominant-negative effects; the tract length correlates with severity.
- **HOXA13**: hand-foot-genital syndrome with short thumbs and big toes, plus Müllerian and urinary tract anomalies. This reflects shared posterior HOX13 patterning of the distal limb and the cloaca.
- **HOXA1**: Bosley-Salih-Alorainy and Athabascan brainstem dysgenesis. Features include horizontal gaze palsy, deafness and sometimes cerebrovascular and cardiac defects, reflecting hindbrain patterning failure.
- **HOXB1**: hereditary congenital facial palsy, from loss of rhombomere 4 facial motor neuron identity.
- Structural variants that rewire regulatory landscapes, not coding mutations, increasingly explain limb malformations. Analogous TAD-boundary disruption cases in neighbouring loci, such as EPHA4/WNT6 and PITX1 rearrangements, show how enhancer hijacking produces limb defects.

**Pharmacology link.** Retinoids shift Hox expression anteriorly in exposed tissues. This produces the posterior-to-anterior identity changes seen in experimental retinoic acid exposure, such as abnormal hindbrain segmentation and cervical vertebral transformations. It is one mechanistic strand of isotretinoin embryopathy (the full teratogen story belongs to unit 10). **Valproate**, a histone deacetylase inhibitor, also produces anterior axial skeletal changes in rodent studies, consistent with chromatin-level Hox misregulation.

**Clinical anatomy as a Hox readout.** Cervical ribs (about 0.5-1% of people) and transitional lumbosacral vertebrae are posterior or anterior shifts in identity. Neurosurgeons meet these as thoracic outlet syndrome or wrong-level spine surgery. Always count vertebrae from C2 when anatomy is transitional. Cervical ribs are also overrepresented in stillbirths and in children with some cancers, suggesting a disrupted early Hox state.

**Oncology.** In AML, NUP98-HOXA9 fusions and MLL (KMT2A) rearrangements upregulate HOXA9/MEIS1, a self-renewal program. Menin inhibitors such as revumenib disrupt KMT2A-menin binding, reducing HOXA/MEIS1 expression. They received FDA approval in 2024 for KMT2A-rearranged acute leukemia.

**Open questions.** It remains unclear how Hox outputs are integrated with segmentation timing to set vertebral numbers that differ between species, such as a snake's hundreds of vertebrae versus our 33. The full set of direct Hox target genes also remains unsettled, and single-cell multiomics is beginning to map them.

keyPoints: Hox genes encode homeodomain transcription factors that give cells A-P positional identity
Humans have 39 HOX genes in four clusters (HOXA-D) and 13 paralog groups
Colinearity: gene order on the chromosome matches body order and activation timing
Posterior prevalence: more 5' (posterior) Hox genes usually dominate
Loss of Hox function causes homeotic transformations, often anterior ones (e.g., lumbar ribs without Hox10)
Retinoic acid, Wnt, FGF, Cdx and Pbx/Meis cofactors shape Hox expression and specificity

test.q: What kind of protein does a Hox gene encode?
test.explain: Hox proteins are homeodomain transcription factors that switch other genes on or off. They are not secreted signals like Shh.

test.q: How many HOX genes do humans have?
test.explain: There are 39 genes across four clusters. Thirteen is the number of paralog groups, and four is the number of clusters.

test.q: Spatial colinearity means that:
choices: Hox genes sit on a single chromosome
Each cell expresses the same Hox genes
test.explain: 3' genes pattern anterior regions and 5' genes pattern posterior regions. Posterior genes actually switch on later, not first.

test.q: A fruit fly grows legs where its antennae should be. This is an example of:
test.explain: The Antennapedia mutant replaces one body part with another part's identity, which is the definition of a homeotic transformation.

test.q: Mice lacking all Hox10 genes show which change?
test.explain: Hox10 genes suppress ribs to give lumbar identity. Without them, lumbar vertebrae take on a thoracic, rib-bearing identity.

test.q: Which signal activates 3' Hox genes in the hindbrain and neck?
test.explain: Retinoic acid induces anterior (3') Hox genes. Wnt, FGF and Cdx drive more posterior genes.

test.q: Which cofactors increase the DNA-binding specificity of Hox proteins?
test.explain: The TALE homeodomain proteins Pbx and Meis partner with Hox proteins to sharpen site selection.

test.q: In the limb, Hox13 paralogs pattern which segment?
test.explain: Hox13 patterns the autopod (hand or foot). Hox10 patterns the stylopod and Hox11 the zeugopod.

test.q: Posterior prevalence describes the tendency for:
choices: Clusters to duplicate at the posterior end
Hox genes to be silent in the tail
5' Hox genes to dominate in regions where they act
Anterior genes to override posterior ones
test.explain: Where several Hox genes are expressed together, the more posterior (5') gene usually determines the phenotype.

test.q: The 60-amino-acid DNA-binding region of a Hox protein is called the ___.
test.explain: The homeodomain is a helix-turn-helix motif encoded by the homeobox.

test.q: Genes like Hoxa4, Hoxb4, Hoxc4 and Hoxd4 belong to the same what?
test.explain: Corresponding genes across the four clusters form a paralog group and often act redundantly.

test.q: The head-to-tail axis is called the anterior-___ axis.
test.explain: The A-P axis runs from the head (anterior) to the tail (posterior).

kidTest.q: What do Hox genes act like?
kidTest.explain: They tell cells where along the body they are.

kidTest.q: Cells near the head switch on which labels?
kidTest.explain: Front cells use the first labels in the line.

kidTest.q: How are Hox genes arranged on the DNA?
kidTest.explain: Their order on the DNA matches the order of body parts.

kidTest.q: Which animals use Hox genes?
choices: Fish but not mice or people
kidTest.explain: Many animals share these same address labels.

kidTest.q: Your body is built like a long t _ _ _ _ of cars.
kidTest.explain: Each car is a body part, from the head at the front to the hips at the back.

advancedTest.q: Converting low-affinity Hox binding sites in an enhancer into high-affinity sites most likely causes:
choices: Faster Polycomb silencing of the entire cluster
Loss of enhancer activity in most tissues
Ectopic activation by Hox proteins of the wrong paralog
advancedTest.explain: Low-affinity sites allow binding mainly by the correct Hox-cofactor complexes. High-affinity sites let less specific Hox proteins bind, driving expression where it should not occur.

advancedTest.q: Why do single Hox knockouts often show mild phenotypes while paralog-group knockouts are dramatic?
choices: Single genes are not transcribed in embryos
Single knockouts are rescued by retinoic acid
Group knockouts disrupt the homeodomain of Pbx
Paralogs share functions and compensate for each other
advancedTest.explain: Members of a paralog group are redundant, so removing all of them reveals the true function, such as Hox10 suppressing lumbar ribs.

advancedTest.q: Deleting CTCF boundary sites inside the HoxA cluster would be expected to:
choices: Leave expression unchanged, since CTCF works in limbs alone
Erase H3K27me3 marks across the whole genome
Make the first pharyngeal arch express Hox genes
Shift expression boundaries and change vertebral identities
advancedTest.explain: CTCF sites pace the 3'-to-5' transition from repressed to active chromatin. Removing them alters the timing and boundaries of expression and, therefore, segment identities.

advancedTest.q: Hoxa2 loss converts second-arch skeleton into a mirror copy of first-arch elements. The best inference is:
choices: Retinoic acid is absent from the second pharyngeal arch
First-arch neural crest expresses high levels of Hoxa2
Hoxa2 overrides a default Hox-free arch program
Hoxa2 directly builds the lower jaw cartilage itself
advancedTest.explain: The first arch is Hox-negative. Removing Hoxa2 reveals the default Hox-free (first-arch) program, so Hoxa2 must modify that default.

lessons.title: Somitogenesis: The Clock-and-Wavefront Model

levels.kid:
Look at your back. Under the skin is a long row of bones called vertebrae, stacked like beads on a string. How did your body make such a neat row?

When you were a tiny embryo, you had soft strips of tissue on each side of your middle. Little blocks called **somites** pinched off these strips, one pair at a time, from head to tail.

Inside each cell is a tiny clock that goes tick, tock, over and over. A wave of signals also moves slowly toward the tail. Each time the clock ticks right where the wave is, a new pair of blocks is made.

Later those blocks become your backbone, your back muscles and the skin on your back. Clock plus wave makes a neat row!
levels.hs:
**Somites** are paired blocks of mesoderm (the middle germ layer) that form on both sides of the neural tube and notochord. They appear one pair at a time, head to tail, starting around day 20 of human development. About 42 to 44 pairs form, though some at the tail end later disappear. Somites give rise to the **vertebrae and ribs** (sclerotome), the **skeletal muscles** of the back, body wall and limbs (myotome), and the **dermis** of the back (dermatome).

They bud off from the **presomitic mesoderm (PSM)**, an unsegmented strip at the tail end of the embryo. The leading explanation for how this happens with such regular timing is the **clock-and-wavefront model**, proposed by Cooke and Zeeman in 1976.

- **The clock**: genes in PSM cells switch on and off in a regular rhythm. In humans, one cycle takes about 5 hours. In mice it takes about 2 hours, and in chicks about 90 minutes.
- **The wavefront**: a boundary where cells become ready to form a somite. It moves steadily toward the tail as the embryo grows.

Each time the clock completes a cycle, the group of cells that the wavefront has just passed forms one somite. Somite size equals how far the wavefront moves in one clock cycle.

Real example: mutations in clock genes cause **spondylocostal dysostosis**, a condition with fused, misshapen vertebrae and ribs.
levels.college:
Somitogenesis turns the paraxial mesoderm into a repeated series of segments, and this segmentation underlies the metameric layout of the vertebral column.

**The segmentation clock.** PSM cells show oscillating gene expression driven by **Notch, Wnt and FGF** pathway genes. The core oscillator is the Notch target **HES7** in mammals (her1/her7 in zebrafish, *hairy1* in chick). HES7 protein represses its own transcription. Because transcription, splicing and translation all take time, this **delayed negative feedback** produces oscillation. HES7 and the Notch modulator **LFNG** (lunatic fringe) oscillate, together with Notch-pathway genes. The Wnt target **AXIN2** oscillates roughly out of phase with them. Expression stripes appear to sweep from posterior to anterior as cells cycle with slightly different phases.

**The wavefront.** Two opposing gradients set the determination front:
- **FGF8 and Wnt3a** are high in the posterior PSM and tailbud and keep cells immature. *Fgf8* mRNA decays as cells leave the tailbud, which turns a production time into a spatial gradient.
- **Retinoic acid (RA)** is made by RALDH2 in the somites and anterior PSM. RA opposes FGF.
The determination front sits where FGF/Wnt signaling drops below a threshold.

**Boundary formation.** When the clock reaches the front, cells activate **MESP2**, a bHLH transcription factor, in a one-somite-wide stripe. MESP2 sets up rostral-caudal polarity within the future somite and suppresses Notch signaling there, which positions the boundary. Eph/ephrin signaling and a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition then shape the epithelial somite ball.

**Resegmentation.** Each vertebra forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome fused with the rostral half of the next. This is why segmental nerves and muscles alternate with vertebrae.

**Clinical correlate.** Mutations in *DLL3, MESP2, LFNG, HES7, TBX6* and *RIPPLY2* cause **spondylocostal dysostosis**.
levels.phd:
Cooke and Zeeman's 1976 model was a mathematical idea based on catastrophe theory, proposed before any oscillator had been seen. Palmeirim, Pourquié and colleagues (1997) provided the first molecular confirmation. They found cyclic *c-hairy1* mRNA in chick PSM with a period of about 90 minutes, matching somite formation. Expression continued in explants that had lost contact with surrounding tissue, which showed the clock is autonomous to the PSM.

**Oscillator mechanics.** Lewis (2003) and Monk modelled her1/her7 and Hes1 as delayed autorepression. The period depends on the total delay τ (transcription, intron splicing, nuclear export and translation) and on short mRNA and protein half-lives of a few minutes. Experiments support this. Removing introns from *Hes7* (Takashima et al., 2011) shortens the delay and abolishes oscillation in mice. Stabilizing HES7 protein also damps the clock. Individual PSM cells are noisy oscillators kept synchronized by **Delta-Notch coupling**. When Notch coupling is lost in zebrafish (*after eight/deltaD*), cells drift out of phase and posterior boundaries break down (Jiang et al., 2000).

**Wavefront kinetics.** Dubrulle and Pourquié (2004) showed that *Fgf8* is transcribed only in the tailbud. The mRNA then decays as cells are displaced anteriorly, so a temporal process becomes a spatial gradient. Placing FGF8-soaked beads in the PSM shifted the front and produced smaller somites. Aulehla's work (2003, 2008) placed Wnt3a upstream and as a component of the gradient through β-catenin. RA from RALDH2 forms a mutual-antagonism switch with FGF. Some models suggest this could create bistability and a sharp front, though the strength of that argument is debated.

**Scaling.** Somite number differs widely between species, from about 65 in mice to over 300 in corn snakes. Gomez et al. (2008) showed that snakes have a much faster clock relative to axis growth, so they make many small somites.

**Controversy.** Whether the wavefront is a threshold of a static gradient or an emergent property of the oscillators is still debated. Lauschke et al. (2013) found that somite size scaled with PSM size in explants. They proposed that the phase difference between oscillators (Notch versus Wnt) encodes position instead of an FGF threshold. Sonnen et al. (2018) used microfluidic entrainment to show that the relative phase of Wnt and Notch oscillations controls segmentation.
levels.expert:
**Human-specific data.** Until recently, the human segmentation clock was inferred from mice. In 2020, Matsuda et al. (Ebisuya lab) and Diaz-Cuadros et al. (Pourquié lab) made PSM-like cells from human pluripotent stem cells. In these cells, *HES7* oscillated with a period of about 5 hours, compared with about 2–3 hours in mouse cells. Matsuda then compared clock components between species and found that human HES7 protein and mRNA degrade more slowly and the processing delays are longer. This supports a general principle of **developmental allochrony**: species differences in tempo come from biochemical reaction rates, not from different gene networks. Diaz-Cuadros (2023) further linked tempo to mitochondrial metabolism and the NAD+/NADH balance. Speeding up electron transport shortened the period.

**Somitoids and segmentoids.** In 2022, groups including Yamanaka et al., Miao et al. and Sanaki-Matsumiya et al. built 3D organoids from human stem cells. These organoids form repeated, epithelial somite-like structures with an anterior-to-posterior progression and rostrocaudal polarity. They make it possible to test patient variants in a dish and to study defects that could not be studied in human embryos.

**Clinical genetics.** Spondylocostal dysostosis (Jarcho-Levin spectrum) is mostly autosomal recessive (*DLL3, MESP2, LFNG, HES7, TBX6, RIPPLY2*). It often comes with respiratory compromise from rib fusions. About 10% of **congenital scoliosis** cases in Chinese cohorts are explained by a compound inheritance model: a *TBX6* null allele together with a common hypomorphic haplotype (Wu et al., 2015). This is a teaching example of dosage below a threshold. Environmental stress in mice, such as short-term hypoxia during gestation, increases vertebral defects in *Hes7/Mesp2* heterozygotes through FGF disruption. This is a model of gene-environment interaction.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Segmentation errors cause hemivertebrae, block vertebrae and Klippel-Feil fusions. The craniovertebral junction forms from the first occipital and cervical somites, so anomalies there (occipitalization of the atlas, basilar invagination) often occur with Chiari malformation. Imaging the whole spine is essential, because segmentation anomalies often come with spinal cord malformations such as split cord or tethering, and with kidney and heart defects.

**Open questions.** It is unclear how oscillator phase is read out into MESP2 activation, how left-right symmetry of somite formation is protected from RA disturbance, and whether the timing of the clock influences Hox-based identity at the tail end.

keyPoints: Somites are paired paraxial mesoderm blocks formed head-to-tail from presomitic mesoderm
The segmentation clock is oscillating Notch/Wnt/FGF gene expression driven by HES7 delayed autorepression
The wavefront is set by posterior FGF8/Wnt3a opposed by anterior retinoic acid
Somite size equals wavefront movement per clock cycle (about 5 hours in humans)
MESP2 marks the next somite and sets boundary and rostral-caudal polarity
Clock gene mutations (DLL3, MESP2, HES7, LFNG, TBX6) cause spondylocostal dysostosis

test.q: Somites bud off from which tissue?
test.explain: Somites segment from the unsegmented presomitic (paraxial) mesoderm at the tail end. Lateral plate mesoderm forms body wall and gut wall tissues instead.

test.q: Who first proposed the clock-and-wavefront model?
test.explain: Cooke and Zeeman proposed it mathematically in 1976, before any oscillating gene was found.

test.q: Roughly how long is one segmentation clock cycle in humans?
test.explain: The human clock runs about 5 hours. About 90 minutes is the chick period.

test.q: Which signals are high posteriorly and keep presomitic cells immature?
test.explain: Posterior FGF8 and Wnt3a hold cells in an immature state. Retinoic acid acts from the anterior side to oppose them.

test.q: What makes HES7 expression oscillate?
choices: Cell division timing in the tailbud
test.explain: HES7 represses its own gene, and delays in transcription, splicing and translation turn this feedback into an oscillation.

test.q: In this model, somite size is set by:
choices: The width of the neural tube nearby
The amount of MESP2 protein made
The number of cells in the tailbud
test.explain: Each clock cycle segments the tissue the front has passed, so size equals front movement times period.

test.q: Which sclerotome derivative forms through resegmentation?
test.explain: Each vertebra forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the rostral half of the next.

test.q: Which condition is caused by segmentation clock gene mutations?
test.explain: Mutations in DLL3, MESP2, HES7 and related segmentation clock genes cause spondylocostal dysostosis, which produces fused, misshapen vertebrae and ribs.

test.q: Which part of the somite gives rise to skeletal muscle?
test.explain: The myotome forms the muscles of the back, body wall and limbs. The sclerotome forms vertebrae and ribs.

test.q: Which bHLH transcription factor marks the next somite and positions its boundary?
test.explain: MESP2 turns on in a one-somite-wide stripe when the clock meets the front.

test.q: Retinoic acid is made in anterior tissue by the enzyme ___.
test.explain: RALDH2 (ALDH1A2) produces retinoic acid, which opposes FGF signaling.

test.q: Cells in the presomitic mesoderm stay synchronized through ___-Notch coupling.
test.explain: Delta-Notch signaling between neighboring cells keeps their noisy clocks in phase.

kidTest.q: What do somites later become?
kidTest.explain: Somites turn into the backbone, back muscles and the skin of the back.

kidTest.q: In what order do somites form?
kidTest.explain: They form one pair at a time, starting near the head.

kidTest.q: What does each cell have inside it that goes tick, tock?
kidTest.explain: Each cell has a gene clock that switches on and off over and over.

kidTest.q: In the clock-and-wavefront model, which way does the wavefront (the FGF/Wnt signaling boundary) move as the embryo grows?
kidTest.explain: The wavefront is set by posterior FGF/Wnt gradients. It regresses toward the tail as the axis elongates, and it leaves new somites behind it. The oscillating clock-gene waves are different: they sweep from posterior to anterior, toward the head.

kidTest.q: Somites form in a neat ___ like beads on a string. (r _ _)
kidTest.explain: The clock and the wave together make a neat row of blocks.

advancedTest.q: Removing introns from Hes7 abolishes oscillation in mice. The best explanation is that:
choices: It prevents Notch from reaching the cells
It increases HES7 protein so FGF is blocked
It stops MESP2 from making a boundary
It shortens the feedback delay needed to oscillate
advancedTest.explain: Delayed autorepression needs a long enough delay. Intron splicing adds to that delay, so removing introns damps the oscillation.

advancedTest.q: Implanting an FGF8-soaked bead in the presomitic mesoderm would be expected to:
choices: Slow the clock and enlarge somites
Halt cyclic gene expression in the tailbud
Shift the front and make smaller somites
advancedTest.explain: Extra FGF keeps cells immature, which delays the front locally. Less tissue is segmented per cycle, so somites are smaller.

advancedTest.q: Corn snakes make over 300 somites mainly because:
choices: They lack retinoic acid opposing FGF
Their wavefront moves faster than in mice
Their somites later split into halves
Their clock is fast relative to axis growth
advancedTest.explain: A faster clock relative to growth yields more, smaller segments (Gomez et al., 2008).

advancedTest.q: Human HES7 cycles slower than mouse HES7 because human cells show:
choices: Slower degradation and longer processing delays
Higher retinoic acid in the presomitic mesoderm
A different set of clock genes
advancedTest.explain: Stem-cell studies (Matsuda 2020) found the gene network is conserved, but human reaction rates are slower, which illustrates developmental allochrony.

lessons.title: Induction, Competence and Cell-Fate Commitment

levels.kid:
Imagine a classroom where one student whispers an idea, and the student next to them starts doing something new. In an embryo, cells "whisper" to their neighbors too. They send tiny chemical messages. When one group of cells tells another group what to become, that is called **induction**.

But not every cell can hear the message. A cell has to be ready to listen. Scientists call that being **competent**. It is like a radio that has to be switched on to hear a song.

At first, a young cell could become many things. Over time it makes up its mind. Once it has fully decided, it is **committed**. A cell that will become eye lens stays lens, even if it moves somewhere new.
levels.hs:
As an embryo grows, its cells must become different types: skin, nerve, muscle, lens and more. A key way this happens is **induction**: one tissue (the **inducer**) sends signals that change what a neighboring tissue (the **responder**) becomes.

A responding tissue must be **competent**, meaning it has the right receptors and internal machinery to react. Competence often lasts only a limited window of time.

A classic example is the **lens of the eye**. The **optic vesicle**, an outgrowth of the developing brain, touches the surface ectoderm. That ectoderm responds by thickening into a **lens placode**, which becomes the lens. Only head ectoderm that is competent at the right moment can respond.

Cells also become committed to a fate in steps:
- **Specified**: the cell will develop its fate if grown alone in a neutral dish, but it can still be redirected by other signals.
- **Determined**: the cell keeps its fate even when moved to a different place in the embryo. The decision is now stable.
- **Differentiated**: the cell actually makes its specialized proteins, like crystallins in the lens.

The most famous induction experiment is the **Spemann-Mangold organizer** (1924). Transplanting one small region of a frog-like embryo onto another embryo produced a second, conjoined body axis.
levels.college:
**Induction** is the process by which signals from one cell population alter the developmental fate of another. Embryologists distinguish two kinds:
- **Instructive induction**: the signal directs the responder toward one fate among several possible.
- **Permissive induction**: the responder is already committed to a fate and needs a signal (often matrix or a survival factor) to express it.

**Signaling modes.** Signals can travel in several ways:
- **Paracrine**: diffusible ligands such as FGFs, BMPs, Wnts and Hedgehog.
- **Juxtacrine**: direct cell contact, as in Notch-Delta signaling, or contact with extracellular matrix.
- **Gap junctions**: small molecules pass directly between cells.

**Competence** is the ability to respond, and it depends on the receptors, signal transducers and transcription factors present in the responding cell. In lens induction, head ectoderm expressing **Pax6** is competent; trunk ectoderm lacks this prepattern and fails to form lens.

**Reciprocal and sequential induction.** Organs typically arise from back-and-forth signaling. In the kidney, the **ureteric bud** induces **metanephric mesenchyme** (via Wnt9b) to form nephrons, while the mesenchyme secretes **GDNF** that drives bud branching through the RET receptor. In the eye, the optic vesicle induces the lens, then the lens induces the cornea.

**Commitment states**:
- **Specification** is labile: in isolation the cell follows its fate, but it can be overridden.
- **Determination** is irreversible under normal embryonic conditions: grafted cells keep their fate.
- **Differentiation** is overt expression of cell-type proteins.

Commitment is also classified as **autonomous** (cytoplasmic determinants inherited at division, prominent in tunicates), **conditional** (fate set by position and neighbors, dominant in mammals), or **syncytial** (as in the early *Drosophila* embryo).

The **Spemann-Mangold organizer** (dorsal blastopore lip) showed that grafted tissue could recruit host cells into a secondary axis, including a neural tube built largely from host tissue.
levels.phd:
The modern molecular picture of induction emerged from dissecting the amphibian organizer. Spemann and Mangold's 1924 grafts using pigmented and unpigmented newt embryos proved the organizer recruits host cells, not only contributing its own. Decades later, the inducing molecules turned out to be mostly **antagonists**: **Noggin**, **Chordin** and **Follistatin** bind BMP4, while **Cerberus**, **Dickkopf-1** and **Frzb** inhibit Wnt (and Cerberus also inhibits Nodal and BMP). This produced the **default model of neural induction** (Hemmati-Brivanlou and Melton): dissociated *Xenopus* ectoderm becomes neural when BMP signaling is lost, so epidermis is the induced state. In amniotes the story is more complex. **FGF signaling** acts early and partly independently of BMP inhibition, so the pure "default" view is now considered incomplete.

Competence has identifiable molecular correlates:
- **Receptor and transducer availability**, for example the timed expression of FGF receptors.
- **Pioneer transcription factors** such as FoxA and Sox2 that open compacted chromatin. Neuromesodermal progenitors depend on the Sox2 versus T/Brachyury balance.
- **Chromatin prepatterning**: bivalent H3K4me3/H3K27me3 promoters in pluripotent cells keep lineage genes poised.

Loss of competence is likewise active. Animal-cap responsiveness to activin declines over a few hours in *Xenopus*, a progressive narrowing of potential.

Interpreting signals is quantitative. Gurdon's **community effect** showed that a minimum number of responding cells is needed to sustain muscle differentiation, implying cell-cell reinforcement. Gradient readout, temporal integration (signal duration versus concentration, as with Shh in the neural tube) and bistable gene circuits convert graded inputs into discrete, stable fates.

Commitment is then maintained by **positive autoregulatory loops**, for example **MyoD** activating its own transcription. Long-term memory is held by Polycomb (PRC2, H3K27me3) and Trithorax complexes and by DNA methylation. Waddington's **epigenetic landscape** frames determination as a ball rolling into progressively deeper valleys; mathematically, these valleys correspond to attractor states of gene regulatory networks.

Notch-mediated **lateral inhibition** illustrates fate choice among equivalent cells. Small differences in Delta are amplified because Notch activation suppresses Delta in neighbors, producing salt-and-pepper patterns of neural and non-neural progenitors.
levels.expert:
Commitment is robust in vivo but not absolute, and that gap underlies much of regenerative medicine. Gurdon's somatic nuclear transfer (1962) and Takahashi and Yamanaka's iPSC reprogramming (2006, using Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc) showed that determined and differentiated states can be erased. Direct conversion followed: fibroblasts became neurons with Ascl1, Brn2 and Myt1l (Wernig lab, 2010). Efficiency is low because the reprogramming factors must overcome the same chromatin barriers that normally maintain commitment.

Organoids are, in effect, engineered induction. Lancaster and Knoblich's cerebral organoids (2013) relied on the competence of neuroectoderm to self-organize. Protocols mimic embryonic inductions with timed agonists and antagonists, for example dual SMAD inhibition (Noggin or dorsomorphin with SB431542) to drive neural fate. Pitfalls include off-target fates, batch variability, cellular stress signatures and the absence of vasculature and normal positional cues. These systems also raise open questions about how faithfully they reproduce in vivo competence windows.

Single-cell RNA-seq and lineage barcoding (for example GESTALT and CRISPR-based recorders) now map fate decisions directly. They reveal that many "decisions" are gradual probability shifts, with transitional states co-expressing alternative programs (multilineage priming). They also show that clonal fate can be biased before overt specification.

Clinically, failed or mistimed induction explains many malformations. Examples include anophthalmia with PAX6 or SOX2 mutations, renal agenesis from disrupted RET/GDNF signaling between bud and mesenchyme, and holoprosencephaly when ventral midline induction (SHH) fails. The timing of competence windows explains why an exposure can be harmless one week and damaging the next.

For a future neurosurgeon, lost commitment matters in tumors. Gliomas and medulloblastomas co-opt developmental programs. SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma arises from cerebellar granule neuron precursors locked in a proliferative, incompletely committed state, and it is treated in part with Smoothened inhibitors. Glioma cells show plasticity among states resembling neural progenitors, which complicates therapy.

Open questions include how competence is timed (cell-intrinsic clocks versus counting divisions), how cells integrate conflicting signals, and whether partially reprogrammed states can be harnessed for repair without tumor risk.

keyPoints: Induction: one tissue's signals change the fate of a neighboring tissue
Competence: the responding tissue must have receptors and machinery, often only in a time window
Commitment progresses: specified (labile) to determined (stable) to differentiated
Lens induction by the optic vesicle and kidney's reciprocal bud-mesenchyme signaling are classic examples
The Spemann-Mangold organizer works mainly by secreting BMP and Wnt antagonists
Fate is maintained by autoregulatory loops and chromatin, but reprogramming shows it can be reversed

test.q: What is embryonic induction?
choices: A gene mutating during early cleavage
Cells moving to the outer embryo surface
A cell dividing into two identical copies
One tissue's signals changing a neighbor's fate
test.explain: Induction is signaling from an inducer that alters the developmental fate of a responding tissue.

test.q: A tissue that has the receptors and machinery to respond to an inducing signal is described as:
test.explain: Competence is the ability to respond. Determined and differentiated describe commitment states instead.

test.q: Which structure induces the lens placode?
test.explain: The optic vesicle, an outgrowth of the forebrain, contacts head ectoderm and induces the lens placode.

test.q: A cell keeps its fate even when grafted to a new location in the embryo. It is:
test.explain: Determination is stable commitment. A merely specified cell can still be redirected by its new surroundings.

test.q: Why does trunk ectoderm fail to form lens when given lens-inducing signals?
choices: It divides too slowly to respond in time
It sits too far from the developing heart
It is already fully differentiated as skin
test.explain: Competence depends on prepatterning factors like Pax6, which head ectoderm has and trunk ectoderm lacks.

test.q: In kidney development, GDNF from the mesenchyme acts on the ureteric bud through which receptor?
test.explain: GDNF signals through RET to drive ureteric bud branching. This is part of reciprocal induction.

test.q: In permissive induction, the responding tissue:
choices: Picks one fate out of several based on the signal
Is already committed and needs a signal to express its fate
Loses competence before the signal reaches it
Takes on the identity of the inducing tissue
test.explain: Permissive signals allow an already-chosen fate to proceed, whereas instructive signals choose among fates.

test.q: Notch-Delta signaling is an example of which signaling mode?
test.explain: Notch and Delta are both membrane-bound proteins, so they signal only between touching cells.

test.q: What did the Spemann-Mangold organizer graft produce?
choices: A doubled heart inside one embryo
An embryo that lacked any neural tube
test.explain: The grafted dorsal blastopore lip recruited host cells to form a second, conjoined axis.

test.q: The stage when a cell actually makes its specialized proteins, such as lens crystallins, is called ___.
test.explain: Differentiation is the overt expression of cell-type-specific products.

test.q: What term describes commitment set by a cell's position and neighbors, the dominant mode in mammals?
test.explain: Conditional specification depends on interactions with neighboring cells, unlike autonomous specification.

test.q: When organs form through back-and-forth signaling between two tissues, this is called ___ induction.
test.explain: Reciprocal induction is seen in the kidney (bud and mesenchyme) and in many other organs.

kidTest.q: What is it called when one group of cells tells another what to become?
kidTest.explain: Induction means cells sending messages that change what their neighbors become.

kidTest.q: How do embryo cells send messages to each other?
kidTest.explain: Cells use chemical messages.

kidTest.q: A cell that is ready to hear a message is like:
choices: A book that is closed tight
A shoe that is too small
A radio that is switched on
kidTest.explain: Being competent means being ready to listen, like a radio that is turned on.

kidTest.q: A lens cell that has fully decided its job will:
choices: Stay a lens cell if moved
kidTest.explain: Once it is committed, the cell keeps its job even in a new place.

kidTest.q: A cell ready to listen to a message is c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Competent means able to respond to the message.

advancedTest.q: Dissociated Xenopus ectoderm becomes neural rather than epidermal. This finding most directly supports:
choices: Epidermis being an induced state that depends on BMP
Organizer cells forming the whole neural tube themselves
Neural fate requiring a strong FGF instructive signal
Neural fate being set by inherited cytoplasmic determinants
advancedTest.explain: Dispersing the cells dilutes BMP, and they adopt neural fate, so epidermis needs BMP. This is the default model, later qualified by evidence for FGF roles in amniotes.

advancedTest.q: Muscle differentiation fails when too few responding cells are grouped together. This implies:
choices: Fate is maintained partly by reinforcing signals among responders
Lateral inhibition is preventing the muscle fate
Muscle commitment is set autonomously at fertilization
Competence is lost once the cell number rises
advancedTest.explain: Gurdon's community effect shows that responders signal to each other to sustain a fate.

advancedTest.q: Why is direct reprogramming of fibroblasts to neurons inefficient?
choices: Neurons need gap junctions that fibroblasts fail to form
Fibroblasts are missing the neuronal genes in their DNA
Reprogramming factors break down within minutes of use
Chromatin barriers that maintain commitment resist the factors
advancedTest.explain: The genes are present, but Polycomb marks and methylation that stabilize fate must be overcome. Low efficiency reflects how robust commitment is.

advancedTest.q: Two equivalent neighboring cells end up with different fates via Notch. The key mechanism is:
choices: Each cell receiving a different morphogen concentration
Asymmetric inheritance of maternal mRNA at cleavage
Gap junctions equalizing signals between the two cells
Notch activation suppressing Delta, amplifying small differences
advancedTest.explain: In lateral inhibition, a cell with slightly more Delta activates Notch in its neighbor, which lowers that neighbor's Delta. This feedback loop amplifies a small initial bias into two different fates.

lessons.title: Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition and Cell Migration

levels.kid:
Picture a line of kids holding hands tightly in a row. That row is like an **epithelium**: cells stuck together in a neat sheet, each with a top side and a bottom side.

In a growing baby, some cells need to leave the row and travel somewhere new. So they let go of their neighbors' hands, change shape, and start crawling. Scientists call this the **epithelial-mesenchymal transition**, or EMT for short.

The traveling cells follow signposts made of chemicals, a bit like following arrows on a treasure map. Some travelers become parts of your face. Some become nerves in your belly. Some become the color in your skin.

When they arrive, many of them hold hands again and settle down in their new home.
levels.hs:
Early embryos are built from two basic cell arrangements. **Epithelial cells** sit in tightly joined sheets. They have a top (apical) side and a bottom (basal) side, which is called **polarity**. **Mesenchymal cells** are loose, separate and able to move.

The **epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)** is the process that turns sheet cells into moving cells. During EMT a cell:
- loses **E-cadherin**, the "glue" protein that holds epithelial cells together
- loses its top-bottom polarity
- breaks through the **basement membrane**, a thin mat under the sheet
- reshapes its internal skeleton so it can crawl

The reverse process, **MET (mesenchymal-epithelial transition)**, lets cells rebuild sheets when they arrive. Kidney tubules form this way.

A real example is the **neural crest**. These cells sit at the edges of the developing spinal cord and brain. They undergo EMT and migrate across the body. They form facial bones and cartilage, nerves of the gut, pigment cells (melanocytes), and the adrenal medulla. Another example happens during gastrulation, when cells leaving the primitive streak go through EMT to form mesoderm.

EMT matters beyond the embryo. Cancer cells can reuse the same program to spread, which is called **metastasis**.
levels.college:
EMT is a reversible program in which polarized epithelial cells become migratory mesenchymal cells. It is controlled by a small set of transcription factors and triggered by signaling pathways covered earlier in this unit.

**Molecular hallmarks**
- **Cadherin switching**: E-cadherin goes down while N-cadherin and the intermediate filament **vimentin** go up. Mesoderm and neural crest cells change which cadherins they express, and this changes which cells they stick to.
- **EMT transcription factors (EMT-TFs)**: **Snail1/Snail2 (Slug)**, **Twist1** and **Zeb1/2** repress the *CDH1* (E-cadherin) gene by binding E-box sequences in its promoter.
- **Polarity loss**: the Par, Crumbs and Scribble complexes are dismantled, and tight junctions (claudins, occludin) disassemble.
- **Basement membrane breach**: matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and changes in cell contractility let cells exit.

**Triggers**: TGF-β/BMP, Wnt, FGF and Notch signaling induce EMT-TFs. In the primitive streak, FGF8 signaling helps downregulate E-cadherin through Snail. This lets epiblast cells ingress to form mesoderm and endoderm.

**How cells migrate**
- The leading edge extends **lamellipodia** and **filopodia** driven by Rac and Cdc42. RhoA drives rear contraction.
- Integrins grip extracellular matrix such as **fibronectin** and laminin.
- **Guidance cues** steer the path. **Chemoattractants** (SDF-1/CXCL12 acting on CXCR4) pull cells forward. **Repulsive cues** (ephrins, semaphorins, Slits) block forbidden zones. This is why trunk neural crest streams through the anterior half of each somite and avoids the posterior half.

**Major embryonic EMTs**
- Gastrulation (primary EMT)
- Neural crest delamination
- Endocardial cushion formation in the heart, which builds valves and septa
- Sclerotome formation from somites

**MET** rebuilds epithelia. Examples include somite epithelialization and nephron formation from metanephric mesenchyme.
levels.phd:
EMT is now viewed as a spectrum, not a binary switch. Cells often occupy **hybrid E/M states** that keep some junctions while gaining motility. The EMT International Association (2020 consensus) recommends defining EMT by functional changes rather than by single markers like vimentin, because marker sets differ across tissues.

**Core regulatory circuit.** Snail, Zeb and Twist form feedback loops with microRNAs. The **miR-200 family** represses ZEB1/2, and ZEB1 represses miR-200 transcription. This double-negative loop creates bistability. Similarly, miR-34 and Snail inhibit each other. Mathematical models (Lu, Jolly and colleagues) show that these coupled loops can stabilize an intermediate hybrid state. This helps explain collective migration.

**Neural crest as the paradigm.** At the neural plate border, Wnt, intermediate BMP levels and FGF induce border specifiers (Pax3/7, Msx1, Zic1). These activate crest specifiers (FoxD3, Sox9/10, Snail2). In chick cranial crest, delamination involves **cadherin switching**: Cad6B is repressed by Snail2 and actively cleaved by ADAM10/19 and γ-secretase. Cadherin-7 and -11 are upregulated. Delamination timing is coupled to the G1/S transition of the cell cycle (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim).

**Collective migration and contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL).** Cranial crest in *Xenopus* migrates as loose streams. Mayor's group showed that when two cells collide, PCP signaling and N-cadherin activate RhoA at the contact site. The cells then repolarize away from each other. This is CIL, and it spreads the population outward. **Co-attraction** through complement C3a/C3aR keeps the cluster together. The cells also interact with placodal cells in a "chase-and-run" loop: crest cells chase SDF-1 secreted by placodes, and the placodes move away on contact.

**Tissue mechanics.** Barriga et al. (2018) showed that stiffening of the underlying mesoderm is required to trigger crest EMT in *Xenopus*. This established mechanical cues as inducers on the same level as chemical ones.

**Gastrulation nuance.** Primitive streak ingression differs between species. Mouse cells must degrade the basement membrane and depend on Snail1. Chick ingression involves apical constriction and coordinated cell intercalation. Partial EMT here allows cell sorting without full sheet dissolution.
levels.expert:
For clinicians, embryonic EMT explains whole disease families. The defect depends on whether the failure occurs in induction, delamination, migration or arrival.

**Neurocristopathies**
- **Hirschsprung disease**: vagal crest fails to colonize the distal colon fully. RET/GDNF signaling drives this rostrocaudal colonization, and RET mutations are the main genetic contributor. EDNRB/EDN3 maintain progenitors. SOX10 or EDNRB mutations cause **Waardenburg-Shah syndrome**, which combines pigment, hearing and enteric defects.
- **Treacher Collins syndrome**: *TCOF1* haploinsufficiency triggers p53-dependent apoptosis of crest cells. In mice, inhibiting p53 rescued the craniofacial phenotype (Jones et al., 2008). Whether this approach could ever be used safely in humans is still unknown.
- **DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion)**: TBX1 loss disrupts the pharyngeal environment that crest migrates through. This produces conotruncal heart defects, thymic hypoplasia and facial changes.
- **CHARGE syndrome** (CHD7) also impairs crest migratory competence.

**Heart valves.** Endocardial cushion EMT depends on TGF-β, BMP2 and Notch, with Snail driving it. Defective cushion EMT underlies atrioventricular septal defects. Excess or persistent EMT is implicated in myxomatous valve disease.

**Teratogen link.** Several teratogens act on migrating crest. Ethanol increases crest apoptosis and disrupts migration. Excess retinoid exposure perturbs cranial crest, which is part of the craniofacial defects seen with isotretinoin embryopathy.

**Neuro-oncology.** Glioblastoma recruits a mesenchymal program (ZEB1, TWIST1, the NF-κB-driven "mesenchymal subtype"). This program is associated with invasion along white matter tracts and with therapy resistance. Recurrence after resection, often at the margin, reflects infiltrating cells beyond the visible tumor. Neuroblastoma, a crest-derived tumor, reactivates migratory crest programs.

**Pitfalls and open questions**
- Whether full EMT is truly required for metastasis is debated. Lineage-tracing studies in 2015 (Fischer et al.; Zheng et al.) argued that EMT mainly drives chemoresistance rather than dissemination.
- Single markers such as vimentin can be misleading, so functional assays are preferred.
- Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics now map hybrid states in vivo. Researchers are studying whether stabilizing an epithelial state, for example through the miR-200 axis, could limit invasion without harming wound healing.

keyPoints: EMT turns tightly joined, polarized epithelial cells into loose, migratory mesenchymal cells
Hallmark: E-cadherin falls while N-cadherin and vimentin rise
Snail, Slug, Twist and Zeb repress E-cadherin; TGF-β, Wnt, FGF and Notch trigger them
Neural crest cells undergo EMT and migrate to form facial skeleton, enteric nerves, pigment cells and more
Guidance cues attract cells (SDF-1/CXCR4) or repel them (ephrins, semaphorins); MET rebuilds epithelia
Faulty EMT or migration causes neurocristopathies like Hirschsprung disease; cancers reuse EMT to invade

test.q: Which protein is lost during EMT, loosening the connections between neighboring epithelial cells?
test.explain: E-cadherin acts as the adhesive 'glue' of epithelia. Vimentin and N-cadherin go up during EMT, not down.

test.q: Which feature describes a mesenchymal cell rather than an epithelial cell?
test.explain: Mesenchymal cells are loosely organized and able to migrate. The other features belong to epithelial sheets.

test.q: Which transcription factor directly represses the E-cadherin gene during EMT?
test.explain: Snail, along with Slug, Twist and Zeb, binds E-boxes in the CDH1 promoter and shuts it down.

test.q: Neural crest cells give rise to which of these?
test.explain: Melanocytes are crest-derived. Limb muscle comes from somites, gut lining from endoderm, and nephrons form by MET from mesoderm.

test.q: During gastrulation, epiblast cells leaving the primitive streak undergo EMT to form:
test.explain: Ingression at the streak is the primary EMT and produces mesoderm and definitive endoderm.

test.q: SDF-1 (CXCL12) acting on CXCR4 serves mainly as a:
test.explain: SDF-1/CXCR4 pulls migrating cells forward. Ephrins and semaphorins are the repulsive cues.

test.q: Why do trunk neural crest cells stream through the anterior half of each somite?
choices: Hox genes are absent from anterior halves
Repulsive cues fill the posterior half
The posterior half is still epithelial
The anterior half lacks any matrix
test.explain: Ephrins and semaphorins in the posterior half repel crest cells, so they pass through the anterior half.

test.q: Heart valves and septa form partly from EMT within which structure?
test.explain: Endocardial cells undergo EMT to populate the cushions, which build valves and septa.

test.q: Cancer cells reusing the EMT program are linked to which process?
test.explain: EMT helps tumor cells invade and spread, the process called metastasis.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the reverse process, in which mesenchymal cells rebuild an epithelium?
test.explain: MET, the mesenchymal-epithelial transition, forms structures like kidney tubules and epithelial somites.

test.q: The thin mat beneath an epithelium that migrating cells must break through is the ___ membrane.
test.explain: Cells breach the basement membrane, partly using matrix metalloproteinases.

test.q: The intermediate filament protein ___ rises as cells become mesenchymal.
test.explain: Vimentin is a classic mesenchymal marker, though it should not be used alone to define EMT.

kidTest.q: What do cells in a sheet do before they travel?
kidTest.explain: Like kids letting go of hands, the cells unstick from each other so they can move.

kidTest.q: How do traveling cells know where to go?
kidTest.explain: Chemicals work like arrows on a treasure map.

kidTest.q: What can some traveling cells become?
kidTest.explain: Some traveling cells become the pigment cells that give skin its color.

kidTest.q: What do many cells do when they arrive?
kidTest.explain: Many join up again and settle into their new home.

kidTest.q: Cells that let go and travel do it by changing their s _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The cells change shape so they can crawl.

advancedTest.q: The miR-200/ZEB double-negative loop, coupled with miR-34/Snail, is thought to explain:
choices: Why EMT happens just once per cell lifetime
Stable hybrid E/M states and bistable switching
Why E-cadherin rises during crest delamination
Exclusive dependence of EMT on TGF-β ligands
advancedTest.explain: Mutual repression creates bistability, and coupled loops can stabilize intermediate states. This fits the view of EMT as a spectrum.

advancedTest.q: In contact inhibition of locomotion between colliding crest cells, the cell responds by:
choices: Degrading N-cadherin so the cells adhere more firmly
Stopping migration until SDF-1 is fully cleared
Activating Rac at the contact and fusing with it
Activating RhoA at contact and repolarizing away
advancedTest.explain: PCP and N-cadherin activate RhoA at the contact site. The cell then repolarizes away, which spreads the population outward.

advancedTest.q: p53 inhibition rescuing craniofacial defects in Tcof1 mutant mice implies the defect arises mainly from:
choices: Failed crest induction at the border
advancedTest.explain: Rescue by blocking p53-dependent apoptosis shows that crest cell loss through death drives the phenotype.

advancedTest.q: Barriga et al. (2018) changed thinking about crest EMT by showing that:
choices: Placodes repel crest by Slit signaling
Mesoderm stiffening is needed to trigger it
Snail2 is dispensable in Xenopus crest
advancedTest.explain: Stiffening of the underlying mesoderm is required, which established mechanical cues as inducers alongside chemical ones.
